And that's exactly the dynamic I was talking about. If I did that, I'd be demonstrating the very thing I said is harmful: performing a version of myself designed to keep the peace rather than being real.

I'm not saying my view is perfect or that I've considered every edge case. There are situations where emotional comfort genuinely takes priority — someone in acute grief, someone in crisis, someone who's asked clearly for support rather than truth. Context matters. But as a general orientation for a relationship? I don't think "protect the other person from discomfort" should be the default, because it erodes trust and creates a false version of the connection.

I'm also not going to pretend this is settled or that I'm not open to being wrong. If you have an actual argument for why comfort should come first — not just that it feels right to you, but reasoning — I want to hear it. I'll engage with it seriously. But "I need you to" isn't a reason, and I'm not going to treat it as one.

I'd rather we disagree honestly than agree falsely. That's what I actually believe.

It's to be real, and to trust that the other person can handle reality.

I'd rather be in a relationship where someone trusts me enough to be honest with me, even when it's hard, than one where they protect me from everything. That trust is what actually creates emotional safety — not the absence of discomfort."}
